html:
A stepped temple tower at Ur in southern Iraq, built about 2100 BCE by King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur and finished by his son Shulgi. It is the best preserved ziggurat in Mesopotamia.

It was the high place of Nanna, the moon god and patron of Ur. Its solid core was mud brick, faced with baked bricks set in bitumen. Three great stairways met at the top of the first stage, and a shrine probably stood on the summit. It was not a tomb or a hall but a man made mountain that lifted the temple toward the sky.

Ur-Nammu also issued the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code known. The ziggurat crumbled and was rebuilt by the Babylonian king Nabonidus in the 500s BCE. Leonard Woolley excavated it in the 1920s and 1930s, and its lower facade was rebuilt in the 1980s. It stands near Nasiriyah, a short walk from the Royal Cemetery where the Royal Game of Ur was found.
